LANG_PRIOR_quote: The earliest Proto-Elamite inscriptions, being purely ideographic, do not in fact contain any linguistic information nor is it known what language was spoken in the area during the Proto-Elamite Period.
VALUES_quote: This is because certain signs, notably a majority of the numerical signs, are similar to the neighboring Mesopotamian proto-cuneiform.
notes: LANG_PRIOR: accounts conflict (Mnamon says the language is assumed to be an ancient form of Elamite; Wikipedia says no positive evidence and language unknown); coded from Wikipedia. CORPUS: about 1,600-1,700 tablets stated but no typical length, so NS.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: According to common theory, Canaanites or Hyksos who spoke a Canaanite language repurposed Egyptian hieroglyphs to construct a different script.
ANCHOR_quote: Likewise, this allowed another recurring word mʿhbʿlt to be translated as "Beloved of (the) Lady", a reading which became very acceptable after the lemma was found carved underneath a hieroglyphic inscription which read "Beloved of Hathor, Lady of Turquoise".
VALUES_quote: Based on the similarity to Phoenician letters and hieroglyphic signs, he suggested that these Sinai inscriptions were alphabetic and that they were linked to Egyptian hieroglyphic signs based on acrophony.
WORDDIV_quote: The poor conservation of the inscriptions, their brevity and the absence of separation marks between two grammatical units all strongly penalize decipherment.
CORPUS_quote: More than thirty Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions have been found.
notes: CORPUS: multiplied about 30-40 inscriptions by the stated lengths (some three or four signs, some longer), giving under 1,000 signs.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: There are three serious obstacles to decipherment, assuming rongorongo is truly writing: the small number of remaining texts, the lack of context such as illustrations in which to interpret them, and the poor attestation of the Old Rapa Nui language, since modern Rapa Nui is heavily mixed with Tahitian and is therefore unlikely to closely reflect the language of the tablets.
ANCHOR_quote: Assuming that rongorongo is writing, there are three serious obstacles to decipherment: the small number of remaining texts, comprising only 15,000 legible glyphs; the lack of context in which to interpret the texts, such as illustrations or parallel texts which can be read; and the fact that the modern Rapa Nui language is heavily mixed with Tahitian and is unlikely to closely reflect the language of the tablets—especially if they record a specialized register such as incantations—while the few remaining examples of the old language are heavily restricted in genre and may not correspond well to the tablets either.
WORDDIV_quote: Fischer notes that the long text of the 125-cm Santiago Staff is unlike other texts in that it appears to have punctuation: The 2,320-glyph text is divided by "103 vertical lines at odd intervals" which do not occur on any of the tablets.
CORPUS_quote: The 26 rongorongo texts with letter codes are inscribed on wooden objects, each with between 2 and 2320 simple glyphs and components of compound glyphs, for over 15,000 in all.
notes: LANG_PRIOR 1: Old Rapa Nui is the assumed language, but the account says it is not settled that rongorongo is writing at all. WORDDIV 0: only the Santiago Staff has dividing lines, and they are not said to mark words. VALUES: only a claimed link to the unread Indus script is reported.

LANG_HIND_quote: Safaitic (Arabic: ٱلصَّفَائِيَّة Al-Ṣafāʾiyyah) is a variety of the South Semitic scripts that was used by the Arabs in southern Syria and northern Jordan in the Ḥarrah region, to carve rock inscriptions in various dialects of Old Arabic and Ancient North Arabian.
WORDDIV_quote: The inscriptions can be written in nearly any direction and there are no word dividers.
notes: CORPUS: counts of inscriptions only (about 30,000 in Wikipedia, about 35,000 in Mnamon), no typical length, so no band (at least C). Accounts do not describe what was held in 1901 about language, names or sign values.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: Salomon determined that there are a sufficient number of shell characters to represent the syllables of the Sanskrit language, and tentatively assigned sounds to some of characters.
ANCHOR_quote: In a few instances, shell inscriptions are paired with Brāhmī letters, as in the example at Deogarh, Uttar Pradesh, illustrated here.
VALUES_quote: B. N. Mukherjee subsequently proposed a system of decipherment based on a few key inscriptions using the assumptions that the script is an ornamental form of the contemporary Brahmi script through the centuries.
notes: ANCHOR: the account says shell inscriptions are paired with Brahmi letters on the same object but does not say the Brahmi text is a version of the shell text. CORPUS: length given (no more than ten to twelve syllables) but no count of inscriptions.

LANG_HIND_quote: Sidetic was probably closely related to Lydian, Carian and Lycian.
ANCHOR_quote: It was only after the discovery of a second Greek-Sidetic bilingual inscription in 1949, that Hellmut Theodor Bossert was able to identify 14 letters of the Sidetic script using the two bilinguals.
VALUES_quote: The Sidetic alphabet has 31 identified letters, a few of which are clearly derived from Greek.
notes: LANG_PRIOR: account says the script was assumed to write the indigenous language of Side (Arrian), which names no known language or family, so NS. WORDDIV: vertical strokes read as word dividers by a minority only, so NS. CORPUS: no sign or length figures.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: Because the phonetic decipherment stage is not finished, it is difficult to establish what language the script represents.
VALUES_quote: If a letter appears to be of Phoenician origin and has a similar phonetic value in both Phoenician and other Paleohispanic scripts, that phonetic value is assumed to be the same in the southwestern script.
notes: CORPUS: nearly a hundred stelae, longest 86 characters, no typical length; band cannot be fixed between A and B.

LANG_PRIOR: the account names the Tangut language and cites the History of Song (1346) for the script's creation but does not say what scholars held in the 1930s. LANG_HIND: no relative of Tangut is named. ANCHOR: bilingual diplomatic documents and translations from Tibetan and Chinese are mentioned as historical practice, not as objects known at T. VALUES: characters are said to resemble Chinese in appearance but to be formed differently; no statement on values.

LANG_HIND_quote: It emerged c. 1400 or 1300 BCE to write Ugaritic, an extinct Northwest Semitic language, and fell out of use amid the Late Bronze Age collapse c. 1190 BCE.
WORDDIV_quote: The only punctuation is a word divider which is often not used.[citation needed]
notes: WORDDIV: accounts conflict; Wikipedia says the word divider is often not used, Mnamon says most texts use a small vertical wedge as word separator; coded from Wikipedia. ANCHOR: Mnamon reports parallel-column lists (Sumerian, Akkadian, Ugaritic) and tablet KTU 5.14 giving Akkadian signs for each letter, but neither account says these were known at T (1930), so NS. CORPUS: nearly 2000 texts and fragments, no typical length.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: According to Urcid (2005), the script was originally a logo-syllabic system and was probably developed for an ancient version of contemporary Zapotecan languages, but its application to language varieties other than "Ancient Zapotec" encouraged the development of logophonic traits.
ANCHOR_quote: Some of the places listed on Building J slabs have been tentatively identified, and in one case (the Cañada de Cuicatlán region in northern Oaxaca) Zapotec conquest has been confirmed through archaeological survey and excavations.
notes: ANCHOR: place identifications on the Building J slabs are tentative and, per the account, recently contested.
